change.author: Joe Au-Yeung

findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with a zod SafeParse result
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` result (`{success, data}`), not the parsed data. Line 97 assigns it to `key` and then writes `data: { key }` to the credential. Every Google token refresh therefore stores `{success:true,data:{...}}` in place of the credential, which destroys the stored tokens. Use `.data`. Separately, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response` on the sync path, so `res?.data` on line 94 is undefined there.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys that evaluate to "[object Object]"
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to the string `"[object Object]"`, not a wildcard key. The schema therefore requires a numeric property literally named `"[object Object]"`, and no token response has one. Whenever credential sync is enabled, every refresh fails with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The 'any number is the expiry' behaviour needs `.passthrough()` and a custom refine. Line 26 also injects a fake `refresh_token` of "refresh_token" into the data, which is later persisted for callers that store `.data`.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response and sends no authentication
findings.body: The sync branch returns a fetch `Response`. Callers that use axios (zohocrm, zoho-bigin, hubspot, google) read `.data` on the result, which is undefined for a `Response`, so they crash. The request also carries no secret header, so the endpoint cannot verify the caller. There is no error handling, no timeout and no JSON parsing.

findings.title: credentialId is passed where a userId is expected
findings.body: The third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId`. Passing `credentialId` makes the sync endpoint receive a credential id as `calcomUserId`, so it looks up the wrong user's tokens or fails. Pass the credential's `userId`.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes the token on every connection and bypasses the sync path
findings.body: The new unconditional `fetch` to login.salesforce.com runs each time a connection is created. It does not use `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is ignored. It adds a network round trip and a DB write per call. The `response.statusText !== "OK"` check is fragile, because HTTP/2 responses have an empty statusText. Line 92 says `!accessTokenParsed.success`, but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on failure, so that branch is dead.

findings.title: Parse failures now throw, and the error logging was removed
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on an invalid response. The old code logged the zod error and the MS response and continued, and the `!tokenResponse.success` branch has been deleted. Because the function throws, `tokenResponse.success` is always true afterwards. The refresh now fails hard, with no diagnostic information.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==`, and input errors surface as 500
findings.body: The secret comparison is not constant-time. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` (line 57) all throw unhandled on bad input, producing 500s instead of 400s. Use `safeParse` and a try/catch.

findings.title: Credential-sync response is saved as the whole credential key without parsing
findings.body: With credential sharing on, `refreshOAuthTokens` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15) returns the sync endpoint's response. Its comment says that response holds only the access token and expiry. Lines 77-93 then run `handleErrorsJson` on it and write it to `credential.key` with `prisma.credential.update`. Nothing here uses `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, which exists to fill in a placeholder `refresh_token`. The stored key therefore loses `refresh_token`, and the sync endpoint's expiry field is probably not `expires_in`. The result is `expiry_date = now + 0`, so the token counts as expired on the next call. Parse the sync response, keep the existing `refresh_token`, and handle the expiry field name. This path has no test.

findings.title: Sync-endpoint response will fail the strict Webex refresh schema
findings.body: With credential sharing on, `response` comes from the sync endpoint, which returns only the access token and expiry. `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (lines 49-56) requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. The parse at line 88 fails and every refresh rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". The shared `parseRefreshTokenResponse` helper, which handles the sync shape, is not used here. Use it, or skip the strict schema in sync mode.

findings.title: Lark sync response is parsed as a Lark API envelope
findings.body: With credential sharing on, `resp` comes from the sync endpoint. Line 84 runs `handleLarkError` on it and then reads `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in` and `data.data.expires_in` (lines 87-95). Those fields only exist in Lark's own response envelope. A sync response with just an access token and expiry would throw a TypeError on `data.data`. If it did not throw, it would write undefined or NaN values into the stored credential. Branch on sync mode, or parse the sync response with `parseRefreshTokenResponse`.

contracts.action: Lark token refresh now goes through refreshOAuthTokens, which may call CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT instead of Lark
contracts.equivalent_path: packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts, and the Google and HubSpot call sites
contracts.before_after: Before, it always fetched Lark directly. Now, when sync is enabled and `userId` is set, it fetches the sync endpoint, and the unchanged Lark-envelope parsing and DB write follow.
contracts.visible_effect: Calendar calls fail, or the credential is overwritten with bad data, when sync is on.
contracts.failure_mode: The `data.data` access throws. The error is logged and rethrown at line 109-110.

contracts.action: office365video and webex refresh via refreshOAuthTokens
contracts.before_after: The sibling flows parse the sync response with `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. These two do not.
contracts.visible_effect: Meeting creation fails, or the stored key loses its refresh_token.
contracts.failure_mode: Webex rejects on its strict schema. office365video overwrites the key with the sync response.

summary:
**Batch 1 of 1.** The credential-sync change breaks token refresh in several places. Google overwrites the stored credential with a zod result object. The minimum token schema can never validate. `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `Response` where callers read `.data`. Zoho Bigin passes a credential id as a user id. Salesforce now refreshes on every connection. The new webhook is missing input validation and constant-time comparison. I judged all of this from the diff and read none of the files in full, so each finding rests on the diff alone.

**Batch 1 of 1, retry.** The import-path moves to `_utils/oauth/` are consistent: the old paths have no remaining references, and the new files exist. The `zoho-bigin` redirectUri hardcode matches its config slug. The slugs `msteams` and `lark-calendar` match their app metadata. The real problem is the new `refreshOAuthTokens` wrapping in office365video, webex and lark. The unchanged downstream code does not handle the sync endpoint's minimal response, so these three apps break when credential sharing is enabled. These three findings rest on the sync endpoint returning only an access token and expiry, as the comment in `refreshOAuthTokens.ts` says, so confidence is medium.
